chapters.title: Remarkable Incident of Doctor Lanyon
paragraphs: Time went by; a reward of thousands of pounds was offered, since the public felt Sir Danvers's death as an injury to itself; but Mr. Hyde had vanished from the knowledge of the police as though he had never existed. A great deal of his past was dug up, and none of it was to his credit: stories emerged of the man's cruelty—as callous as it was violent—of his vile life, his strange companions, and the hatred that seemed to have dogged his whole career; but as to where he now was, not a word. From the moment he left the house in Soho on the morning of the murder, he was simply erased; and gradually, as time passed, Mr. Utterson began to recover from the height of his alarm and to grow easier in his mind. To his way of thinking, the death of Sir Danvers was more than paid for by Mr. Hyde's disappearance. Now that this evil influence had been lifted, a new life began for Dr. Jekyll. He came out of his seclusion, renewed his old friendships, once again became their familiar guest and host; and while he had always been known for his charitable works, he was now no less noted for his religious observance. He kept busy, spent much time outdoors, did good works; his face seemed to open and brighten, as though with an inward sense of service performed; and for more than two months the doctor knew peace.

On the 8th of January Utterson had dined at the doctor's house with a small party; Lanyon had been there too; and their host's face had turned from one to the other just as in the old days when the three of them had been inseparable. On the 12th, and again on the 14th, the door was shut against the lawyer. “The doctor is confined to the house,” Poole told him, “and sees no one.” On the 15th he tried once more and was again turned away; and having grown used, over the past two months, to seeing his friend nearly every day, he found this return to solitude weighing on his spirits. On the fifth night he had Guest in to dine with him; on the sixth he made his way to Dr. Lanyon's.

There at least he was not refused admittance; but once inside, he was shocked at the change that had come over the doctor's appearance. His face had his death sentence written on it plainly. The once ruddy man had grown pale; his flesh had wasted away; he was visibly balder and older; and yet it was not so much these marks of a swift physical decline that caught the lawyer's attention as something in his eye and manner that seemed to speak of some deep terror in his mind. It seemed unlikely that the doctor should fear death; yet that was exactly what Utterson found himself suspecting. “Yes,” he thought; “he is a doctor, he must know his own condition and that his days are numbered; and the knowledge is more than he can bear.” And yet when Utterson remarked on how ill he looked, it was with an air of great resolve that Lanyon declared himself a doomed man.

“I have had a shock,” he said, “and I shall never recover from it. It's a matter of weeks now. Well, life has been pleasant; I liked it; yes, sir, I used to like it. I sometimes think that if we knew everything, we should be glad enough to get away.”
“Jekyll is ill too,” Utterson observed. “Have you seen him?”

But Lanyon's face changed, and he raised a trembling hand. “I want to see or hear no more of Dr. Jekyll,” he said, in a loud, unsteady voice. “I am quite done with that person, and I beg you to spare me any mention of someone I now regard as dead.”
“Tut, tut,” said Mr. Utterson; then, after a considerable pause, “Can't I do anything?” he asked. “We are three very old friends, Lanyon; we shall not live to make others.”
“Nothing can be done,” Lanyon answered. “Ask him yourself.”
“He will not see me,” said the lawyer.

“I am not surprised at that,” came the reply. “Someday, Utterson, after I am dead, you may perhaps come to learn the right and wrong of this. I cannot tell you now. And in the meantime, if you can sit and talk with me of other things, then for God's sake stay and do so; but if you cannot keep off this accursed subject, then in God's name go, for I cannot bear it.”

As soon as he got home, Utterson sat down and wrote to Jekyll, complaining of being shut out of the house and asking the cause of this unhappy break with Lanyon; the next day brought a long reply, worded in places quite movingly, and elsewhere darkly obscure in its meaning. The quarrel with Lanyon was beyond mending. “I do not blame our old friend,” Jekyll wrote, “but I share his view that we must never meet again. From now on I mean to live in the strictest seclusion; you must not be surprised, nor doubt my friendship for you, if my door is often shut even to you. You must let me go my own dark way. I have brought upon myself a punishment and a danger I cannot name. If I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also. I could not have believed this earth held room for suffering and terror so unmanning as this; and there is only one thing you can do, Utterson, to lighten this fate of mine, and that is to respect my silence.” Utterson was amazed; with Hyde's dark influence withdrawn, the doctor had gone back to his old work and old friendships; only a week before, the outlook had promised a cheerful and honoured old age; and now, in a moment, friendship, peace of mind, the entire course of his life lay wrecked. So great and unlooked-for a change suggested madness; but given Lanyon's manner and words, there had to be some deeper cause.

A week later Dr. Lanyon took to his bed, and in under a fortnight he was dead. The night after the funeral, at which he had been deeply moved, Utterson locked the door of his office and, sitting there by the light of a single melancholy candle, drew out and set before him an envelope addressed in the hand and sealed with the seal of his dead friend. “PRIVATE: for the hands of G. J. Utterson ALONE, and in case of his predecease to be destroyed unread”—so it was pointedly marked; and the lawyer dreaded to look at what was inside. “I have buried one friend today,” he thought: “what if this should cost me another?” Then he condemned the fear as disloyal and broke the seal. Inside was a second, sealed enclosure, marked on the cover “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll.” Utterson could hardly believe his eyes. Yes, it said disappearance; here again, just as in the mad will he had long ago returned to its author, here again were the notion of a disappearance and the name of Henry Jekyll linked together. But in the will, that notion had sprung from the sinister suggestion of the man Hyde; it had been set there with a purpose all too plain and horrible. Written in Lanyon's own hand, what could it mean? A great curiosity seized the trustee, to disregard the prohibition and dive straight to the bottom of these mysteries; but professional honour and loyalty to his dead friend were binding obligations, and the packet went to sleep in the innermost corner of his private safe.

It is one thing to hold curiosity in check, another to conquer it altogether; and it may be doubted whether, from that day on, Utterson wished for his surviving friend's company with quite the same eagerness. He thought of him with kindness, but his thoughts were troubled and fearful. He did go to call; but he was perhaps relieved to be turned away; perhaps, in his heart, he preferred to speak with Poole on the doorstep, surrounded by the air and sounds of the open city, rather than be admitted into that house of voluntary imprisonment and sit talking with its unreadable recluse. Poole, in fact, had no very pleasant news to give him. The doctor, it appeared, now confined himself more than ever to the cabinet above the laboratory, where he sometimes even slept; he was low in spirits, had grown very silent, did not read; it seemed as though something weighed on his mind. Utterson grew so used to the unchanging character of these reports that he gradually visited less and less often.

chapters.title: Incident at the Window
paragraphs: It happened on a Sunday, when Mr. Utterson was out on his usual walk with Mr. Enfield, that their route took them once again through the by-street; and when they came to the door, both of them stopped to look at it.
“Well,” said Enfield, “that story is over, at least. We shall never see Mr. Hyde again.”
“I hope not,” said Utterson. “Did I ever tell you that I saw him once myself, and shared your feeling of disgust?”

“It was impossible to feel one without the other,” Enfield replied. “And by the way, what a fool you must have thought me, not knowing that this was a back way into Dr. Jekyll's! It was partly your own fault that I found it out, even when I did.”

“So you did find it out?” said Utterson. “Well, if that's so, we may as well step into the court and take a look at the windows. To tell you the truth, I am uneasy about poor Jekyll; and even from outside, I feel as though a friend's presence might do him good.”

The court was very cool and a little damp, and full of an early twilight, though high overhead the sky was still bright with sunset. The middle one of the three windows was half open; and sitting close beside it, taking the air with an air of boundless sadness, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
“What! Jekyll!” he cried. “I trust you are better.”
“I am very low, Utterson,” the doctor replied drearily, “very low. It will not last long, thank God.”

“You stay indoors too much,” said the lawyer. “You ought to be out, getting your blood moving, like Mr. Enfield and me. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come now, get your hat and take a quick turn with us.”

“You are very kind,” the other sighed. “I should like to very much; but no, no, no, it is quite impossible; I dare not. But indeed, Utterson, I am very glad to see you; this is a real pleasure; I would ask you and Mr. Enfield up, but the place really is not fit.”
“Well, then,” said the lawyer good-naturedly, “the best thing we can do is stay down here and talk with you from where we are.”

“That is just what I was about to suggest,” the doctor answered with a smile. But the words were scarcely out before the smile was wiped from his face and replaced by such an expression of utter terror and despair that it froze the blood of the two men below. They caught only a glimpse of it, for the window was instantly pulled down; but that glimpse was enough, and they turned and left the court without a word. In silence, too, they made their way back through the by-street, and it was not until they had come into a nearby thoroughfare, where even on a Sunday there were still some signs of life, that Mr. Utterson finally turned and looked at his companion. Both were pale, and there was an answering horror in their eyes.
“God forgive us, God forgive us,” said Mr. Utterson.
But Mr. Enfield only nodded very seriously and walked on again in silence.

chapters.title: Dr. Lanyon's Narrative
paragraphs: On the ninth of January, four days ago now, I received in the evening post a registered envelope addressed in the hand of my colleague and old school friend, Henry Jekyll. This surprised me a good deal, since we were by no means in the habit of writing to each other; I had seen the man, in fact dined with him, only the night before, and I could think of nothing in our dealings that would call for the formality of registration. What the letter said only deepened my surprise, for it read as follows:
“10th December, 18—.

“Dear Lanyon,—You are one of my oldest friends; and although we may have differed at times on scientific questions, I cannot remember, at least on my side, any break in our affection. There was never a day when, if you had said to me, ‘Jekyll, my life, my honour, my reason, depend upon you,’ I would not have sacrificed my left hand to help you. Lanyon, my life, my honour, my reason, are all at your mercy; if you fail me tonight, I am lost. You might suppose, after this preface, that I am going to ask you for something dishonourable. Judge for yourself.

“I want you to put off all other engagements for tonight—yes, even if you were summoned to the bedside of an emperor—take a cab, unless your own carriage should be actually at the door, and with this letter in hand for reference, drive straight to my house. Poole, my butler, has his orders; you will find him waiting your arrival with a locksmith. The door of my cabinet is then to be forced, and you are to go in alone; open the glazed press (letter E) on the left, breaking the lock if it is shut, and draw out—with all its contents exactly as they stand—the fourth drawer from the top, or, which comes to the same thing, the third from the bottom. In my extreme distress of mind I have a morbid fear of giving you the wrong directions; but even if I am mistaken, you will know the right drawer by its contents: some powders, a phial, and a notebook. I beg you to carry this drawer back with you to Cavendish Square exactly as it stands.

“That is the first part of what I am asking; now for the second. If you set out at once on receiving this, you should be back long before midnight; but I will leave you that much margin, not only for fear of some obstacle that can neither be prevented nor foreseen, but because an hour when your servants are in bed is better suited to what will then remain to be done. At midnight, then, I ask you to be alone in your consulting room, to admit with your own hand into the house a man who will give my name at the door, and to place in his hands the drawer you will have brought back from my cabinet. Then you will have played your part and earned my gratitude in full. Five minutes afterwards, if you insist on an explanation, you will understand that these arrangements, fantastic as they must appear, are of the utmost importance, and that neglecting even one of them might leave on your conscience my death or the wreck of my reason.

“Confident as I am that you will not make light of this appeal, my heart sinks and my hand trembles at the mere thought of such a possibility. Picture me at this hour, in a strange place, weighed down by a blackness of distress no imagination could exaggerate, and yet well aware that if you will only serve me punctually, my troubles will roll away like a story that is told. Serve me, my dear Lanyon, and save
“Your friend,
“H.J.

“P.S.—I had already sealed this letter when a fresh terror struck upon my soul. It is possible the post office may fail me, and this letter not reach you until tomorrow morning. In that case, dear Lanyon, carry out my errand whenever it is most convenient for you in the course of the day, and once again expect my messenger at midnight. By then it may already be too late; and if that night passes without incident, you will know that you have seen the last of Henry Jekyll.”

On reading this letter, I felt sure my colleague had lost his mind; but until that was proved beyond all doubt, I felt bound to do as he asked. The less I understood of this jumble, the less I was in a position to judge how important it might be; and an appeal worded like this one could not be set aside without taking on a grave responsibility. So I rose from the table, got into a hansom, and drove straight to Jekyll's house. The butler was expecting my arrival; he had received, by the same post as mine, a registered letter of instructions, and had already sent for a locksmith and a carpenter. The tradesmen arrived while we were still talking, and we all moved together to old Dr. Denman's surgical theatre, from which—as you are doubtless aware—Jekyll's private cabinet is most conveniently entered. The door was very strong, the lock excellent; the carpenter admitted he would have great trouble and would have to do much damage if force were used, and the locksmith was near despair. But this last was a capable fellow, and after two hours' work the door stood open. The press marked E was unlocked; I took out the drawer, had it packed with straw and tied up in a sheet, and returned with it to Cavendish Square.

There I proceeded to examine its contents. The powders were made up neatly enough, but not with a dispensing chemist's precision, so it was plain they were of Jekyll's own manufacture; and when I opened one of the wrappers I found what seemed to me a simple crystalline salt, white in colour. The phial, to which I turned next, might have been about half full of a blood-red liquid, highly pungent to the smell and seeming to contain phosphorus along with some volatile ether. At the other ingredients I could make no guess. The notebook was an ordinary ledger and contained little but a series of dates. These covered a period of many years, but I noticed the entries stopped nearly a year ago, quite abruptly. Here and there a brief remark was added to a date, usually no more than a single word: “double,” occurring perhaps six times in a total of several hundred entries; and once, very early in the list, followed by several exclamation marks, “total failure!!!” All this, though it sharpened my curiosity, told me little that was definite. Here were a phial of some salt and the record of a series of experiments that had led, like too many of Jekyll's investigations, to no end of practical use. How could the presence of these things in my house affect either the honour, the sanity, or the life of my flighty colleague? If his messenger could go to one place, why could he not go to another? And even granting some obstacle, why should this gentleman be received by me in secret? The more I reflected, the more convinced I grew that I was dealing with a case of brain disease; and though I sent my servants off to bed, I loaded an old revolver, so that I might be found in some posture of self-defence.

Twelve o'clock had scarcely finished sounding over London when the knocker sounded, very gently, on the door. I went myself at the summons, and found a small man crouching against the pillars of the portico.
“Are you come from Dr. Jekyll?” I asked.

He told me “yes” by a constrained gesture; and when I had bidden him enter, he did not obey without first casting a searching glance back into the darkness of the square. A policeman was not far off, advancing with his bull's-eye open, and at the sight of him, I thought my visitor started and hurried his steps.

These details struck me, I confess, unpleasantly; and as I followed him into the bright light of the consulting room, I kept my hand ready on my weapon. Here, at last, I had a chance of seeing him clearly. I had never set eyes on him before, that much was certain. He was small, as I have said; and I was struck, besides, by the shocking expression of his face, by his remarkable combination of great muscular energy and great apparent frailty of constitution—and, last but not least, by the odd, personal disturbance his nearness caused in me. This bore some resemblance to the onset of a chill, and came with a marked drop in my pulse. At the time I set it down to some private, idiosyncratic distaste of my own, and merely wondered at how sharp the symptoms were; but I have since come to believe the cause lies far deeper in the nature of man, and turns on some nobler hinge than mere hatred.

This person—who had, from the very first moment of his entrance, stirred in me what I can only describe as a repelled curiosity—was dressed in a fashion that would have made an ordinary man ridiculous; his clothes, that is to say, though of rich and sober fabric, were enormously too large for him in every measurement—the trousers hanging on his legs and rolled up to keep them off the ground, the waist of the coat below his hips, and the collar sprawling wide upon his shoulders. Strange to relate, this absurd getup was far from moving me to laughter. Rather, since there was something abnormal and misshapen in the very essence of the creature now facing me—something arresting, startling, and revolting—this further oddity seemed only to fit with and reinforce it; so that to my interest in the man's nature and character was added a curiosity as to his origin, his life, his fortune, and his standing in the world.
These observations, though they have taken so much space to set down, were the work of only a few seconds. My visitor was, in fact, on fire with a sombre excitement.
“Have you got it?” he cried. “Have you got it?” And so keen was his impatience that he even laid his hand on my arm and tried to shake me.

I pushed him back, aware at his touch of a certain icy pang through my blood. “Come, sir,” I said. “You forget that I have not yet had the pleasure of your acquaintance. Be seated, if you please.” And I showed him an example, taking my own usual seat myself, doing as fair an imitation of my ordinary manner with a patient as the lateness of the hour, the nature of my preoccupations, and the horror I had of my visitor would allow me to manage.

“I beg your pardon, Dr. Lanyon,” he replied civilly enough. “What you say is very fair; my impatience has got the better of my manners. I come here at the request of your colleague, Dr. Henry Jekyll, on a matter of some importance, and I understood…” He paused and put his hand to his throat, and I could see, despite his composed manner, that he was struggling against the onset of hysteria—“I understood, a drawer…”
But here I took pity on my visitor's suspense, and perhaps a little on my own growing curiosity.
“There it is, sir,” I said, pointing to the drawer, where it lay on the floor behind a table, still covered with the sheet.

He sprang toward it, then paused, and pressed his hand to his heart; I could hear his teeth grinding with the convulsive working of his jaw, and his face was so ghastly that I grew alarmed both for his life and his reason.
“Compose yourself,” I said.

He turned a dreadful smile on me, and, as if with the resolve of despair, tore away the sheet. At the sight of what lay inside, he let out one loud sob of such immense relief that I sat there petrified. And the next moment, in a voice already fairly well under control, “Have you a graduated glass?” he asked.
I rose from my place with some effort and gave him what he asked for.

He thanked me with a smiling nod, measured out a few minims of the red tincture, and added one of the powders. The mixture, which was at first a reddish hue, began, as the crystals dissolved, to brighten in colour, to fizz audibly, and to throw off small clouds of vapour. Suddenly, at that same moment, the fizzing stopped and the compound changed to a dark purple, which then faded, more slowly, to a watery green. My visitor, who had watched these changes with a sharp eye, smiled, set the glass down on the table, and then turned and looked at me with an air of scrutiny.

“And now,” he said, “to settle what remains. Will you be wise? Will you be guided? Will you let me take this glass in my hand and go out of your house without further talk? Or has the greed of curiosity too much command of you? Think before you answer, for it shall be as you decide. If you decide as before, you shall be left exactly as you were, neither richer nor wiser, unless the sense of having served a man in mortal distress may be counted as a kind of riches of the soul. Or, if you would rather choose otherwise, a new province of knowledge and new avenues to fame and power shall be laid open to you, here, in this room, upon the instant; and your sight shall be blasted by a marvel to stagger the disbelief of Satan himself.”

“Sir,” I said, affecting a coolness I was far from truly feeling, “you speak in riddles, and you will perhaps not be surprised that I hear you with no very strong impression of belief. But I have gone too far along this road of inexplicable services to stop now before I see the end of it.”

“It is well,” my visitor replied. “Lanyon, remember your vows: what follows is under the seal of our profession. And now, you who have so long been bound to the most narrow and material views, you who have denied the power of transcendental medicine, you who have mocked your betters—behold!”

He put the glass to his lips and drank it down in one gulp. A cry followed; he reeled, staggered, clutched at the table and held on, staring with bloodshot eyes, gasping with open mouth; and as I watched, a change seemed to come over him—he appeared to swell—his face suddenly turned black and his features seemed to melt and shift—and the next moment I had sprung to my feet and leapt back against the wall, my arms raised to shield me from that horror, my mind sinking into terror.

“Oh God!” I screamed, and “Oh God!” again and again; for there before my eyes—pale and shaken, half fainting, groping before him with his hands like a man risen from the dead—there stood Henry Jekyll!

What he told me in the hour that followed, I cannot bring my mind to set down on paper. I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it; and yet now, when that sight has faded from my eyes, I ask myself whether I believe it, and I cannot answer. My life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me; the deadliest terror sits by me at all hours of the day and night; and I feel that my days are numbered, and that I must die; and yet I shall die unconvinced. As for the moral corruption that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror. I will say but one thing, Utterson, and that—if you can bring your mind to believe it—will be more than enough. The creature who crept into my house that night was, on Jekyll's own confession, known by the name of Hyde, and hunted for in every corner of the land as the murderer of Carew.
HASTIE LANYON.
